html:
In about 180 BCE Greek kings of Bactria crossed the Hindu Kush into what is now Pakistan and northwest India. They founded the Indo-Greek kingdoms, which lasted, in shrinking pieces, until about the start of the common era.

These Greeks were heirs of Alexander the Great and of the Seleucid Empire, cut off from the Mediterranean world. The Maurya Empire had just fallen, leaving the northwest open. Demetrius I began the push. The most famous king, Menander, ruled from Sagala, near modern Sialkot, and may have raided deep into the Ganges plain.

Menander lives on in a Buddhist text, the Questions of King Milinda, in which he debates a monk. The Indo-Greeks struck fine coins with Greek on one side and Prakrit on the other, and helped start the meeting of styles that became Gandharan art. Saka and later Kushan invaders from the steppe replaced them.
